Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Four years ago, the farm producer received $4 a bushel for 3CW wheat. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an important and urgent matter.
Considering the necessity of showing all the required objectivity in the discussions on the position of Quebec in the present Canadian federalism; considering that as full Canadian citizens Quebeckers pay federal taxes and that they are not unanimously prepared to see their money spent for political purposes, possibly against their constitutional option; considering that it would be to the benefit of all Canadians to know and study all the realities of the country without any passion, prejudice or electoralism to inquire on the best constitutional formula which could satisfy both major nations which make up this country, and because this option could be the establishment of a new Canada which would be in line with the diversity itself; and considering that the special committee co-ordinated by Mr. Tellier, from the federal-provincial relations branch seems to be used first of all for the political polemic against a government which was elected democratically, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette):
That the federal-provincial relations branch be transformed into an advisory office for objective consultation without any partisanship, to which supporters of the main constitutional formulas presently put forward could refer in all objectivity.

edge of fish stocks and population dynamics. It is in this area that the federal government has the responsibility and expertise, and it should be directing its efforts there rather than to commercial activities which must be the responsibility of the private sector.
The minister announced his decision to close the department's technological laboratories as part of the government's program to cut back expenditures. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member gives me an opportunity to put a few facts on the record. First of all, we are not closing scientific research in any capacity. We are looking at closing a technological branch. In fact, it is the industry's normal responsibility to develop the product that it wants to put in the marketplace. We have very substantially improved our scientific research capacity in stocks and management and will continue to do so.
1 might say, Mr. Speaker, that the article I saw in the Globe and Mail this morning indicates that one company-which is one of the few public companies in fisheries-has tripled its income. Because of our policy, I think the industry is in a position now to do its own technological research.

subsubtopic: CLOSING OF GOVERNMENT RESEARCH LABORATORIES- INQUIRY WHETHER INDUSTRY CONSULTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the need for scientific input has never been greater, due to our extended fisheries' jurisdiction on both coasts and the potential it offers our primary fish processing sector, will the minister indicate, in light of his recent answer, what sections of the work presently being carried out by the laboratories will be turned over to the private sector, and how this transfer will be accomplished so that vital scientific work and the scientists who are now doing it will remain in Canada and be available to all processors?

subsubtopic: CLOSING OF GOVERNMENT RESEARCH LABORATORIES- INQUIRY WHETHER INDUSTRY CONSULTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again I refuse to use the word "scientific". It is technological research; it is not scientific. I have made it clear that in the area of the primary producers-gear and other developments for fishermen-we will not cut down on the program. There are members of an industry who constantly sign letters in which they ask governments to stay away from certain sectors and to spend less money. Now that their profit picture has improved so much, we have asked the industry if they are interested in developing their own products, in which case we would make an orderly transfer to them. I must say they were less enthusiastic about this suggestion than they were about writing letters of protest.

employment situation. Does the minister agree with the Prime Minister, and does he intend to follow his policy? If so, when can we expect an announcement from the minister about the federal fisheries' development program?

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Fisheries. The Fisheries Council of Canada, in their letter of September 22, appealed to the Prime Minister to change the direction of the Department of Fisheries and to change government policy on fisheries. They pointed to the refusal of the minister to issue to Canadians any licences for freezer factory vessels to replace the foreign effort and enable our fishermen to catch new species.
Why is the minister refusing to issue licences for new Canadian freezer factory trawlers, when he is now permitting East German trawlers to land fish at Newfoundland's south coast ports to enable those plants to continue operating, presumably because the plants need the fish? Why will he not permit Canadians to acquire their own trawlers and start that process, in light of the fact he is now allowing foreign vessels to land their fish from the Canadian quota at south coast ports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Fisheries Council and the hon. member did not bother to read a letter which was published in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald and, if my memory is correct, in the St. John's evening Telegram in which I said very clearly that if there were enterprises which wanted licences to catch under-utilized species, and only that, I would be willing to look at their requests.
The fact is that catch rates are still such that the existing fleet can take a very large percentage of the fish available to us in the zone in which we have traditionally fished. The East German landing of fish was done in order to help plants that are undersupplied mainly because of the failure of the Gulf redfish. We made an offer that was open to everyone. Companies that wanted to avail themselves of temporary charters to fish selected stocks, which we had not been taking, were invited to do so. A couple of companies responded; the others did not.

The letter also points out that there is ad hoc manipulation of fishery resources instead of forward-planning for development. There are now more deals in the fishery than in Las Vegas.

Will the minister tell the House why he is permitting East German vessels to fish traditional species and land them in Newfoundland, and why he gave permission to Bulgarian and Russian vessels to take 400 metric tonnes of herring on the northeast coast of Newfoundland, herring that, had it been landed in Newfoundland, could have kept plants operating and men processing fish? Is it because the president of the union- the minister appears to be his puppet-asked for this concession for the Russians and Bulgarians? What is the explanation of this?

Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the hon. member suggests, the East Germans are fishing for northern redfish stocks which we have traditionally not found economical to take. It is being landed in plants that are undersupplied.
On the second point, yes, I did authorize the sale of 400 tonnes, out of the total quota of 20,000 tonnes, to the Russians. I feel that our fishermen and our industry are not getting out of herring, which has become quite a luxury product, the full return which they should be getting. The industry asked me if there was a way of putting in a needle, and I answered yes.

Mr. Speaker, in so far as the government of Newfoundland having to share in the losses of the railway is concerned, I do not believe that that has ever been suggested. Certainly, it is not anything I have ever contemplated in that particular sense and, to the best of my knowledge, the government has never formulated that idea, whatever CN may have said. There is, of course, the broader question of the whole transportation mix of services in Newfoundland and the costsharing between the two levels of government.
On the earlier question, the CN, of course, makes the point that if the revenues and the business is not forthcoming, then one of two things obviously will have to be done, either the trains must operate without having necessarily paying loads- or, indeed, even being filled on some occasions-or somebody other than CN directly must pick up the losses.
The question of auditing the books is one which is now being undertaken by the Sullivan commission. Indeed, I made a specific request, personally, to Mr. Sullivan, after the first volume emerged, that he look into two things, one being the rate structure of Canadian National, to put to rest one way or the other the claims which have been made that, indeed, it is the rate structure that is largely at fault. Perhaps we can now return to the prior but unfinished question of privilege which was raised by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), after which there had been what I took to be a withdrawal by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone). In this regard I refer back to the point raised by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen).
The Chair is often as troubled by withdrawals of offensive remarks in this House as it is by the offensive remarks themselves. I reflect back immediately to three or four occasions upon which I have asked for withdrawals of offensive remarks, and I think the record will show that I have been met with some very ingenious and very qualified withdrawals which, in the circumstances, I have been obliged to accept. Whether I ought to be more insistent on an unqualified withdrawal in these circumstances is a point which I am not at all disinclined to discuss, and on examining this particular instance I refer the Deputy Prime Minister back to three or four cases in recent memory involving the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and, I think, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker).
In those cases statements were made which I said ought to be withdrawn. On all those occasions there were presented to the House and to me a fascinating variety of withdrawals. I think we should examine all of them to see whether or not we should be insistent-I am not afraid of this if it is the will of the House-on a categorical withdrawal, not something that carries with it a qualification. In any case, if the President of Privy Council wishes to argue that point tomorrow, I will be glad to hear him.

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today on a question of privilege arising out
Privilege-Mrs. Holt
of an incident that took place about 1.55 p.m., Tuesday, October 24. The incident, a gross and unseemly assault on me and my office as an hon. member of this House, occurred moments before my scheduled intervention on behalf of thousands of constituents and petitioners before the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission for the express purpose of stopping their harassment of citizens and infringement on the right of free choice on the main cable dial of television in the greater Vancouver area.
I gave notice to you of my wish to raise this matter last Friday, October 27, the earliest opportunity following my return to Ottawa.
My intervention was designed to tell the CRTC that no agency of government must overstep its mandate, that in no way has it a right to diminish or interfere with the freedom of cultural or entertainment choice of the citizens, as it exists now.
Mr. Speaker, I regret that in order to illustrate fully to you the enormity of the offence, I must use, in this House, the explicit language that one commissioner directed at me. However, I feel you can only properly judge the extent and the depth of the contempt by the words he used.
I want to say that I am hardly a neophyte in the world of vulgar, angry men. I have been through the wars of life where men have dominated. In my profession as a writer and reporter I have worked on the streets, in prisons, on skidroads, waterfront-yes, even in exclusive men's clubs and in city newsrooms-where the explicit language of inadequate men is as common as weather talk in a meteorological station.
But I was shocked and stunned when a public servant used assaultive epithets on me as a member of parliament, and thus on my constituents. Some of my constituents were witnesses to the incident, and one actually was struck by a button he seized from my hand and hurled across the space in front of the commissioner's desk.
Mr. Speaker, I will recount the incident and then will give you proof that I was there in my capacity as a member of parliament, that it was an extension of my job here, and, in fact, I could not be here that day because my constituency believed I had a prior duty to serve them before the CRTC in what many B.C. people consider to be a crisis in freedom. Further proof that I was working there before the CRTC instead of here will show in my attendance record this month, as it did in three previous appearances before the CRTC in the past three years. I was acting in my full capacity as a member of parliament.
In the final part of my submission, I will argue the reasons-the law-to show why I feel you should find contempt and a breach of my privilege as a member of this House, and refer this matter to the appropriate committee for action.
I had properly notified the CRTC September 28, 1978, with a hand delivered message to the chairman that I would be appearing as a member of parliament on behalf of my constituents and petitioners in the hearing on October 24, 1978, in Vancouver, on the renewal of cable licences.

October 31, 1978

The chairman himself, in response to a phone call I made to him, scheduled my intervention for 2 p.m., October 24, to accommodate my duty to be back in the House of Commons on the first available flight, the all-night flight, out of Vancouver to Ottawa.
Between numerous other duties, I worked almost 30 hours to prepare and finish my brief in time for the hearing. The zeroxing of the copies for the commissioners was completed by 1.30 p.m. About five minutes before my scheduled 2 p.m. appearance at the witness table I began to distribute copies of my submission to the CRTC commissioners who were drifting in to take their places at the table following the noon recess.
I was wearing one of the 10,000 buttons that had been distributed to my constituents, petitioners and those people who had called at my office for them and who came in to complain to me about the CRTC and its repeated attempts over the past three years to eliminate all American stations from our primary cable dial in greater Vancouver. The button says "CRTC Stay Out of B.C.". As I handed out the briefs several commissioners asked if I could give them a button. At no time, Mr. Speaker, did I offer a button to them. I carried only a few in my purse.
As I reached the centre table, commissioner Real Therrien, who has always been cordial and responsible in our committees on broadcasting and at the CRTC, asked for a button. He said, "The last time we were here you pinned your previous button on me." 1 asked the obvious question, "Would you like me to pin this one on you?" In the good humour that we were sharing, I suggested that it might be wise not to wear it while sitting in Vancouver. He replied that he would like me to pin it on him.
As I reached across the table to fulfil his request, my hand was grabbed, the button taken from it and hurled across the space in front of the table. It struck a constituent who was standing a few feet from me. The assault on her, I have no doubt, was not deliberate. The person who flung this button and made the following statement was later identified to me as Commissioner Roy Faibish.
Mr. Faibish shouted or snarled. I cannot remember the sound, other than it was one of hysterical anger. I do remember what he said, however, "Get that damned button out of here." I said something to the effect, "How dare you? This is still a free country and you are not giving the orders." I remember telling him at some point that the chairman the night before, at the opening of the hearings, had asked for and received a button from me.
He said that he did not care who asked for the button, that I had better get them out of there or he would, in his words "Shove them up your ...". I hesitate to use the word in here, but you know what I mean.

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Again I say I am not a shy person, but I think we should all be concerned that a bureaucrat, a person appointed to serve us, would treat a member that way. I am not new to bad language.
I could think of only one thing to say in rebuttal, "You chauvinist pig, I will take this further". I said during my submission, and it is on the record, and the whole commission heard it, that I would take this incident to the top. I did in fact wire the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) details of this incident and had the message delivered to his desk at 2 p.m. Wednesday, October 25, with a copy to the leader of the government in the Senate, Senator Ray Perrault, who is the minister responsible for my constituency.
I might say that several commissioners apologized to me for what happened, and said that the language was uncalled for and the actions unacceptable.
But, Mr. Speaker, it did not end there. I want to point out further that because of Mr. Faibish's actions I was deprived of the opportunity to deliver my intervention with the normal strength and responsiveness that my constituents have grown to expect. I took my place at the witness table seconds after this incident to deliver my intervention. I was so shaken and angry at the contempt of my duty, this, the highest assignment, which you know best, Mr. Speaker, in the whole of the public service any citizen can accept, that my voice quivered and my hands shook. Friends who were watching the television on monitors at the back of the room expressed surprise later and wondered what had happened, since I had gone in there with confidence and was quite cool. Of course, the newspapers ridiculed my quivering weak voice and angry approach. It may be hard for hon. members to believe that there are times when one is weakened by anger.
When I returned to my duties I was advised Friday by my Vancouver constituency secretary that a friend of Mr. Faibish, his apologist in effect Denny Boyd, had published a statement that, I believe, compounds the contempt and adds to another serious offence against my duties as a member of parliament.
I believe, as a result of what Mr. Faibish did later and what he admitted he did in his statement, my constituents failed to receive a proper, unbiased, and full hearing from the CRTC on October 24 through their member of parliament.
Here is the published corroboration of this in a column in the Vancouver Sun, October 25, 1978, by Denny Boyd:
After the shouting was over and Holt began reading her formal intervention statement, Faibish screwed a plug into his ear and listened to the French translation of her remarks. Faibish is not French; he is bilingual, however, and,
October 31, 1978

at that point, he had heard quite enough of the Holt voice. And after all, freedom of viewing and listening choice is what the CRTC is all about, isn't it?
Thus by his own admission to Boyd, Mr. Faibish treated my representations with bias and contempt. This and other articles were evidence that this public servant nurtured contempt in the media, not only for this member but of parliament itself.
It does not matter a whit whether Roy Faibish likes me or my method and style of serving my constituents. In fact even if he despises me, and obviously he does, it does not change the fact that he must respect the office I hold as an hon. member of this House.

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
I was duly elected in Vancouver-Kingsway to represent the people of Vancouver-Kingsway. This was my fourth appearance before the CRTC in almost four years. Each time I made it clear, as I did in this case, that my constituents and others petitioned me to act in their interest to halt the repeated attempts by the CRTC to remove American television from our rich primary cable dial that we are so fortunate to have in the greater Vancouver area.
We receive six Canadian stations, four commercial American-two of them impaired-and one public broadcasting service. Repeatedly in British Columbia we have had attempts to remove them one after another. Constantly my constituents have written, petitioned, and begged me to work for reversal, which we have succeeded in doing in five different instances. In that respect I was working as a member of parliament here and in Vancouver.
Repeatedly before the broadcasting committee on which I serve, and at these hearings, I have made these complaints clear, as I did before the CRTC, that they were over-stepping their mandate. In these actions and in the interventions, starting January, 1976, I have always stated clearly that I was acting for my constituency and had literally thousands of petitions and letters. I have here a small sample from just this one week before the hearings. These people have asked me to act for them. They have made their anxieties clear to me about their concern over freedom of cultural choice. They have made it clear that big government agencies are diminishing or threatening that freedom, the right of cultural and entertainment choice.
Further and current evidence that I produce to you now to prove that I attended at the October 24 CRTC hearings as a member of parliament is contained in my September 28 notice to the chairman. In it I said:
This is to advise that I wish to intervene on behalf of myself, my constituents and numerous petitioners.
One set of petitions brought into my office is also proof of my appearance as a member of parliament. These petitions contain, I presume, 1,000 to 1,500 names. They are proof that I appeared as requested by constituents and petitioners. It begins simply with the heading "Petition". I quote:
Privilege-Mrs. Holt
Simma Holt, MP will be appearing on behalf of the undersigned at the CRTC licence renewal hearings commencing in Vancouver on October 24, 1978.
It goes on to say:
We demand the right of free choice of television from our cablevision channels.
Possibly the most graphic proof that I was acting as a representative, as a member of this parliament, and that I was seen as such by my constituents, was the writing on an envelope containing a petition requesting that all stations presently on the dial be grandfathered there. It was slipped through the mail slot of my office some time during the night before my CRTC appearance. At the top was a sketch of the button with the words "CRTC stay out of B.C." The letter was addressed to Holt Simma, MP, 303 Knight Road, Vancouver, B.C. At the bottom right hand corner was written:
Thank you Mrs. Holt Simma for fighting for our freedom. We appreciate this very much.
Sincerely A. Nandenberg
The return address was in Vancouver-Kingsway.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that such behaviour toward any citizen, whether member of parliament or private person, by a CRTC commissioner, is totally unacceptable. However, when the witness is a member of parliament, the offence must surely be contempt of this the highest of offices in Canada, and therefore of parliament as a whole.
Certain persons in position of power and influence, of whom Roy Faibish is one, seem unable to conceal their contempt for the elected representatives of the people and the institution of parliament. We have all heard this type of bureaucrat say or imply, "I wish that the members of parliament-or politicians-would stay out of our hair and let us do our job."
It is thus that tyranny by bureaucracy grows. They are not accountable and can do as they wish if they are not stopped. I say that every effort by this parliament, by cabinet, and in this instance by you, Mr. Speaker, must be used to halt this insidious and creeping interference with the lives of the citizens, and to halt contempt of their elected representatives. This may be the start.
Mr. Speaker, I tell you and hon. members that if it is the last thing I do in my life, whether in this place or as a private citizen, I will fight to restore freedom from these kinds of power hungry tyrants whose egos are bigger than their talent.
I must now move on to the law in order to back up these facts.

speechtext:
Hon. ladies and gentlemen, I feel I had to state the facts and the proof before I could state the law. If any of you happen to be worth-while lawyers, I know you will understand.
Privilege in the parliamentary sense is the rights and immunities which are necessary, and indeed essential, for the member to fulfil his or her functions. It is the vehicle without which the member could not properly perform his or her functions. Since parliament could not perform its functions
80065 -421/*

October 31, 1978
Privilege-Mrs. Holt
without the unimpeded use of the services of members, privilege is thus enjoyed by individual members.
When the privilege of an individual member of the Elouse of Commons or when the privileges of the House of Commons have been breached, this constitutes contempt of parliament.
However, apart from these rights and immunities, or specific privileges such as freedom of speech in parliamentary proceedings, by virtue of its penal jurisdiction the House of Commons has the right to punish actions which, while not breaches of any specific privilege, are offences against its authority and dignity. No precedent is required. If the House of Commons decides that such an action is contempt of the House and requires a punishment, no other court will set aside the warrant when expressed in general terms.
In this regard, a member of the House of Commons has the right to go about his or her business or to perform the functions of a member without being molested, intimidated, or obstructed. Any interference constitutes contempt of parliament.
The British House of Commons on June 6, 1780, resolved:
That it is a gross breach of the privilege of this House for any person to obstruct and insult the members of this House in the coming to, or the going from, the House, and to endeavour to compel members by force to declare themselves in favour of, or against any proposition then impending or expected to be brought before the House.
In other words, when a member of the House of Commons is in the course of his or her functions as a member, such as speaking in a parliamentary proceeding and acting in his capacity as a member, that member is protected by certain specific privileges, for example, freedom of speech in a parliamentary proceeding and, in the event of obstruction-

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Order, please. I do not think there is any difficulty about definitions of basic parliamentary privilege. Had it been in respect of a proceeding of this chamber that this event had taken place, there would not be much doubt. The difficulty that the hon. member has, as I am sure she realizes, is that she was appearing, not at a gathering of the House of Commons or even a committee of the House of Commons, which might leave her in a stronger position, but rather before a public board which, while it may in some ways be an emanation of decisions of this House, nevertheless is a board at which the public can appear. Therefore, that is the area in which the hon. member should concentrate in establishing her privilege, that indeed she was there in her capacity as a member of parliament.
The difficulty is it may have happened to any other citizen, a difficulty I say only in respect of her establishing a connection with a long line of cases of parliamentary privilege which have always narrowed and confined it to proceedings of parliament or parliamentary committees-a parliamentary proceeding of some sort.
I want this in no way to be taken as diminishing the evident affront, which may equally be an argument that the hon. member may want to establish, to her, as a member of parliament, which is alarming in its proportions and its clarity,

I am sure, to every member of the House. That, as a contempt, may be argued. However, in terms of the privilege of attending that proceeding, the hon. member ought to concentrate on the fact that this was a proceeding outside the House. I hope she will state her case in that difficulty.

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know it is not an easy task to determine when a member of the House of Commons is acting in the parliamentary capacity or whether, when you are not in this House or in committee, you are still a member of parliament. However, I feel very strongly that when one member is treated with contempt, not just by a newspaper, it is certainly relevant. There have been cases where contempt has been found as a result of newspaper articles. However, this is by an agency appointed by parliament, and involves a servant of parliament and a servant of the people. I feel very strongly that it is an extension of parliament. I know that if I were speaking before a Kiwanis Club or another group, it would be quite different. I should not have the protection. However, if I were assaulted for having voted in this House, it might well be a contempt.
I do not know whether the case of the Attorney General of Ceylon v. de Livera helps my case or not. I would like to present it. If Your Honour feels that I have already taxed the time of the House, I will not go on any longer. However, I would like to cite that case for your consideration. I feel it is such a gross and ugly contempt that further consideration should be given to it. I will not press my time on you if you feel that case will not be worth-while.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext: I only wanted to indicate to the hon. member that it was not the basic definition of privilege that would assist her. Rather, she ought to concentrate on the difficulty that she faces by the evident difference between a proceeding of this House and a public proceeding in which any citizen might participate as a functioning member. I do not wish to restrict the hon. member in any way on any argument she may wish to develop that the behaviour of this member of a public body was contemptuous toward her and therefore contemptuous toward the House, because that seems to be a very strong argument.

subtopic: MRS. HOLT-AFFRONT BY COMMISSIONER FAIBISH, MEMBER OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
I just have a few more points to make, Mr. Speaker. Had I been there just as a citizen I contend that this paid official, whose salary would be voted in this House in supply, would still be in contempt of a citizen, but it was greater contempt when I was really there as part of my job in place of being here. I think I have adequately proved I was there and was accepted there as a member of parliament.
If you would permit me to continue, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that in the case of the Attorney General of Ceylon v. de Livera (1963 A.C.103) the defendants gave money to a member of the Ceylon House of Representatives as an inducement to write to a minister requesting him to abandon a proposal to acquire the defendants' estate. For this they were charged under the Bribery Act which dealt inter alia with
October 31, 1978

offences by people offering gratification to a member to induce him to take some action "in his capacity as such member." The central issue to be decided in the appeal was the interpretation of the phrase "in his capacity as such member." This may be stretching the similarity of the cases, I do not know. But in determining the meaning of this phrase the court threw some light on what proceedings in parliament, or what the real or essential functions of a member are, for the purpose of considerations of privilege.
Given the proper anxiety of the House to confine its own or its members' privileges to the minimum infringement of the liberties of others, it is important to see that those privileges do not cover activities which are not squarely within a member's true functions.
Again, if I were before a board of trade or a similar outside body, I would not expect to have the privileges of the House. But I do feel that as a member, appearing there as I did, and consequently absent from the House, I enjoy certain rights and a certain protection. Similarly, when I am asked by my constituents to intervene before a federal board which was established by and is accountable to parliament for public money, and then, as a member of the House of Commons, I ask and receive permission to present a brief to that board, can one say I am acting only as a private citizen and not in my capacity of a member of the House of Commons? Or, in the words of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, is not my appearance before the CRTC "sufficiently bound up with and analogous to a proceeding in the House as to be properly described as done by a member in his or her capacity as such"?
The difficulty in defining a member of parliament's role is also set out in the judgment in the de Livera case at page 121:
The most, perhaps, that can be said is that despite reluctance to treat a member's privilege as going beyond anything that is essential it is generally recognized that it is impossible to regard his only proper function as a member as being confined to what he does on the floor of the House itself.

I suppose they are entitled to good manners, a reasonable hearing and so forth, but a question of privilege cannot be invoked with respect to any other matter, if there is a question of privilege at all, except matters relating to an appearance before a board or commission of the federal government, created by a federal statute and responsible to report ultimately to the federal parliament. I regret that I understand the distinction very well. It seems to me that we have three problems to deal with in the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt). The first is that the behaviour, described by the hon. member, of a member of a federal commission is distasteful in respect to any person appearing anywhere near a hearing of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission. That directs itself, however, to those who

are responsible for appointments and presumably, therefore, for the conduct of people who are members of that commission. That responsibility lies within this House as well, and therefore it is certainly proper that the matter be brought to the attention of those people to see whether disciplinary action or dismissal results from any member of any public commission behaving in this way.
The second problem is the difficulty of extending the definitions or the parameters of that special privilege which attaches to members of this House because, after all, it has to be remembered that it is a special privilege that attaches to members of this House for one purpose and one purpose only, and that really is to see to it that those who are elected here have the right to do the job which is fundamental to their role as elected members.
The increasingly complex role of members of the House of Commons now draws us more and more into appearances before boards. It draws us into constituency offices and related activities which did not exist only months ago, but to argue that because we have a special privilege in respect to being here, coming here and voting here, and that in addition we have obligations of other kinds and that therefore privileges have to go with us, is an argument which just simply breaks down. It does not follow, and to extend this privilege into other proceedings which are not proceedings of this House would be a step which, I am sure, is not warranted on the precedents as I understand them at the present time.
However, I do not think that relieves us of the third difficulty. The suggestion which troubles me greatly as well as, I am sure, other members of this House, is the suggestion that an elected member of this House, in the circumstances described here this afternoon, was treated in what was obviously a most contemptuous and most abusive manner by a member of a federal public board, and in examining whether this member has been treated with contempt by a person I think we are entitled to take into account the capacity of the member in her appearance there, which was obvious and well advertised, as she argued this afternoon.
In addition, I think we are entitled to take into account the capacity of the person who was delivering what we might consider to be a contempt, his capacity at that time, which surely clothes him with some knowledge and some responsibility in respect to his position. I cannot decide at this moment that there has been in fact contempt of a member of parliament and therefore contempt of the House, but that is an aspect of the argument which I wish to consider, as the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) invited me to do. That is an aspect I want to consider very carefully before coming to a conclusion as to whether the House can address itself to this matter as a question of contempt or privilege, and I will certainly study it very carefully.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
that Bill C-10, to amend the Income Tax Act to provide for a child tax credit and to amend the Family Allowances Act, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill contains one of the most significant social policy reforms of the decade in this country.
On August 24 I announced the measures that form the substance of this bill. At that time I said:
These measures represent a major restructuring of our social programs to provide greater benefits for . .. lower and middle income families with children.
The changes are a significant reform of the child benefit system. They represent an improvement in federal social programs in line with current realities. They demonstrate that it is possible to achieve liberal reform even in the context of restraint in government spending. I am proud to be associated with them.
Support for families with children has been a cornerstone of federal social policy for decades. Let me describe the main elements of the child benefit system in place until now.
Family allowances have been paid monthly to mothers since 1945. In 1974 they were substantially raised and indexed to

increases in prices. They became part of income tax purposes, and thus subject to progressive rates of tax geared to income, to ensure that net benefits were higher for low income families.
In addition, the personal income tax system has provided exemptions in respect of dependent children. There has been one for children under age 16 and a higher one for those over this age. This distinction dates from the days when family allowances were paid only for children under age 16.
In 1977 the government introduced the $50 child tax credit. It was limited to taxpayers with incomes below some $26,000. But it was of no value to those who did not pay any federal tax.
In considering reforms to this existing child benefit system, I wanted to accomplish three things. They are: to make sure government resources were directed to families which needed them most, to couple reductions in government spending with reductions in taxes, and to ensure that the total amount of federal support of families with children was maintained. Along with this, I wanted to make certain that the share of support going to mothers was not eroded.
I have indicated my goals. To achieve them, I am proposing a three point program: first, replacement of the simple income tax credit of $50 per child with a refundable tax credit of $200 per child; second, a reduction in the monthly family allowance to $20 per month; and third, elimination, on a phased basis, of the differential in the basic deduction for children aged 16 and 17.
Now I wish to explain the mechanics of these reforms. I am proposing that the current child tax credit of $50 per child be abolished and replaced by a new one. This new tax credit is $200 per child and, most important, it is refundable. This means it will benefit those who have no tax to pay, as well as those who pay income tax. It means a parent eligible for the child tax credit, but owing no federal tax, will be entitled to a payment from the government. Thus, a parent who has already paid all his or her tax through payroll deduction will receive a cheque from the government. Similarly, those with incomes too low to tax will be paid to prescribed amounts.
It means a parent who owes some tax will be able to offset this against the credit which he or she is entitled to receive. For example, a mother eligible for a child tax credit of $400 and owing no federal tax would get a refund cheque of $400 from the federal government. A mother owing $100 in federal tax and eligible for a child tax credit of $400 would receive a $300 refund cheque. If a mother owes no tax and her husband owes $100 in tax, the mother will still receive $400, and the husband would, pay his own tax.
In addition, benefits are geared to income above the $18,000 level. Full benefits go to families with incomes below $18,000. Above that level, benefits are reduced by 5 per cent of the family income in excess of $18,000, or $50 per $1,000. A family with two children and an income below $18,000 will receive $400. At an income of $20,000, they will receive $300. At $22,000 of income, the credit will be $200, and above
October 31, 1978

$26,000, a family with two children would receive no tax credit. This is a tax cut amounting to some $810 million a year. It goes mainly to lower income families with children, and represents a major new social reform. In fact it will create an increase in disposable incomes for families below the poverty line in the amount of $156 million.
This is the first federal refundable tax credit. Many have criticized tax cuts which failed to help those in need. This government progressively has eliminated taxes on lower income Canadians through measures such as tax indexing and federal tax reduction. Now we are using the tax system in order to go further, actually to supplement the incomes of such families directly. This is a responsible measure designed in a humane and careful way to re-order government priorities to help those in need. But I want to introduce a note of caution here. This bill is not the beginning of a round of social welfare measures disguised as tax reductions. The costs of this program will not balloon out of proportion.
In overhauling the child tax credit, I had the benefit of thorough study and analysis. This study goes back several years. It involved finding out how the tax system might better be used to provide social benefits. First it was the subject of careful analysis in the federal-provincial social security review conducted in 1973. The federal government set up an interdepartmental committee in 1976, headed by my department, to study the possibility of integrating social program payments with the personal income tax system. This committee examined the matter for more than a year, with particular emphasis on the child benefit area. It is this extensive review which forms the basis for the measures before you today.
The second major proposal in the bill is the reduction in family allowance payments to $20 per child per month. The savings in federal expenditures amount to approximately $690 million a year. They will go toward partially financing the new credit to which I have just referred.
[ Translation]
The third change is the elimination of the differential in the amount of exemption for children of ages 16 and 17.
The exemption has been higher for these children because originally they were not eligible for family allowances. Now that family allowances are available to children up to the age of 18, I am proposing to rationalize the exemption system under the Income Tax Act. The amount of exemption will be uniform for all children under the age of 18. However, this change will be phased in. Thus, children who are currently 16 and 17 years of age will continue to qualify for the higher exemption.
The changes that I have outlined are virtually self-financing. The reduction in expenditures is $690 million in 1979-80, with a net reduction in revenue of $655 million. The revenue reduction works out this way. First, the new child tax credit reduces tax revenues by $810 million. As family allowances are reduced there is less tax revenue, some $130 million less. The elimination of the $50 child tax credit saves $260 million
Family Allowances
and the phased elimination of the differential in the exemption for 16 and 17 year old children saves $25 million in the first year. The net reduction in revenues is thus $655 million.
Mr. Speaker, the new tax credit will be claimable by and payable to the person who receives the family allowance. This will normally be the mother. Thus, while mothers face a reduction in family allowance payments they are the beneficiaries of the new credit. Essentially, these measures will aim federal child benefits at those who need them most. This is accomplished without increasing federal financial requirements. It is accomplished out of saved resources. The amount of benefits going to families with below-average incomes is increased by some $200 million. And as I said earlier, it will create an increase in disposable income for families below the poverty level in the amount of $156 million.
Let me give you a few examples of what this credit will do for a family. A family with two children under age 16 and an income of $5,000 will receive $400 under the new credit. The same family will receive $480 in family allowances for a total of $880. This is $194 more than under the current arrangements. For families with $10,000 of income the gain in disposable income from the changes is $159. Mr. Speaker, at the end of my speech I shall table the figures showing what the various amounts will be according to families and net income.
I would like to say a few words about the timing of the introduction of the measures. The reduction in family allowance payments, the elimination of the current $50 child tax credit and the changes to child exemptions start in January, 1979. The new refundable credit is claimable at the time of filing of 1978 tax returns early in 1979, and is applicable to children qualifying at the end of 1978. The purpose of timing the credit in this way is to maintain the cash flow to families. Lower and middle-income families with children will receive the new credit before they experience the full reduction in family allowances.
I expect this will create some additional economic stimulus, both from the fact that more money will be received earlier and because more of the benefits are directed to lower-income families, those who naturally spend all money they may receive.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to detail for hon. members some of the major features of the new tax credit. First, children eligible for the credit are all those in respect of whom family allowances are payable at the end of the taxation year. This will be all children who are below age 18 at the end of the year. A child born in the year will be eligible for full credit. A child who turns 18 in the year will be eligible for the higher tax exemption that will remain for those of this age.
Second, the credit will be claimable by and payable to the person who receives the family allowance. In most cases this is the mother. Fathers will claim credit in families where there is no mother. Forms for claiming credit benefits will be mailed to family allowance recipients early in 1979.

October 31, 1978
Family Allowances
Third, the amount of the credit will be indexed in a fashion similar to the current indexing of tax exemptions and brackets. The benefits to lower and middle-income families will not be eroded by inflation. Family allowance payments will continue to be indexed as well.
Fourth, the amount of the credit is related to the family's income. Family income is defined to include the income of both spouses supporting the child. This ensures an equitable pattern of benefits. The computation of the credit has been kept as simple as possible. Income will be net income as already determined on the tax form. Families will indicate the number of eligible children and the amount of family income and will claim the resulting benefits.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word about the way the credit benefits will be payable to families. Benefits will first serve to reduce any tax otherwise payable by the person who claims the credit. Any amount of credit left over will be paid in full to the claimant at the time of processing of tax returns.
Mr. Speaker, I have detailed the proposals contained in this bill. I have outlined their effects with some care. I believe this is warranted in describing what amounts to a major overhaul of the child benefit system. This bill is fully in line with the commitments the government has set for itself. These were outlined in the address of the Prime Minister on August 1. The measures are a re-ordering of social priorities to better aim benefits to lower and middle-income families, using only saved resources. At the same time, the measures are equitable. The refundable child tax credit, based on family income, is a response to today's priorities through innovative tax policy. It deserves the support of all members of this House.
I would like to seek the unanimous consent of the House at this time to table three tables outlining the way in which the proposed changes will operate and their effect on government revenues and expenditures.

speechtext:
It is right and fitting, Mr. Speaker, apart altogether from satisfying a legal technicality, that this bill should be introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). I have great respect for the Minister of Finance, but he has not a great liking for honourable gentlemen. He has not had an easy time of it, and I am delighted that he has had this opportunity, the first in a long time, to get up in the House and give us some good news, at least news which will be substantially good for a number of Canadians.
I say at the outset that it is my party's intention to support this bill. We look forward to an opportunity to probe the minister's remarks he has made, and the documents that he has tabled, as we get into committee of the whole. The minister referred to the fact that this was the most significant social policy reform of the past decade. That is an interesting observation, because if you examine the record of this government over the past decade you will find a number of significant social reform measures brought to the House.
Many of the reforms of this government have been presented as the be all and end all, or a kind of panacea to cover the problems of equitable and just income distribution in this country, especially to low income earners. In 1965 there was the declaration by the government of a war on poverty. It was an obvious recognition at the time that something was not quite right in our society, that there were people who were falling behind, and that there was a significant proportion of our population who were living below the poverty line, who were being denied an adequate income to provide them and their families with a healthy environment and an adequately nutritious diet.
Then we come up to some of the later social reforms. The bill now before the House, which is being amended, was brought in, as the minister indicated, in 1974. It significantly amended the universal Family Allowances Act by providing for increases in the amount of the universal family allowance payment, added the youth allowance provisions, and provided for indexing to cope with the inflationary situation. That, of course, was in addition to the new unemployment insurance program which was introduced at about the same time, another significant social reform designed to address this inequitable situation in our society whereby a number of our fellow citizens were falling behind. The gap was widening; the poor seemed to be getting poorer and, in fact, seemed to be
October 31, 1978

getting more numerous. We know what happened to that reform, commendable though it may be.
I understand that later this week we will be faced with further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. We know what happened with respect to the administration of that act. We know that this is the second time since the new bill was introduced that the House has been called upon to change it significantly, either to curtail abuses or cut down on the amount of benefits or tighten up on the qualifications and method of paying benefits.
The fact is that all of these reforms seem to be brought in as a response to the moment without any means of adequate preparation, any adequate study, any adequate forecasting, any adequate-and I do not apologize to my friends on the left-planning. We just go from one ad hoc significant social reform to another, like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who goes from one dairy policy to another, so that we never know from one year to the next exactly what the position is in Canada. As far as the production of food in this country is concerned, the result is nothing short of catastrophic.
I state that, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is significant and relevant that this bill is introduced by the Minister of Finance. I would refer the minister and the House to the Senate Study on Poverty in Canada, sometimes referred to as the Croll committee report, which was tabled in the other place in 1971. At page 171 there appears the following statement:
Poverty is not only the problem of the poor it is the problem for all Canadians. If it is not checked vigorously and solved, not only will the poor continue to suffer, but Canada as a whole will suffer, socially and economically.
Of course, that is true. When we have one million unemployed in this country, our productivity suffers. That is just common sense.
The report continues:
To eliminate poverty in Canada, we must recognize that economic goals such as national economic growth are not ends in themselves but means to the achievement of ends. Without sustained and stable economic growth, Canada could not afford to take the steps which will be necessary to eradicate poverty.
In my view therein lies the answer to the dilemma of the government-why we have to be faced with one significant social reform after another in the eyes of the government. The fact is that the government is not able to create the economic climate in Canada which would make social reform successful, which would help to narrow the gap between the poor and those who seem to get welfare.
In 1974, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian economy stopped growing at a great rate. The 3.7 per cent rate of growth for that year was less than half that of the year before. It fell to as low as 1.1 per cent in 1975, which economists told us was the equivalent of zero growth. We have had a less than 5 per cent rate of growth in the last five years and we are unlikely to achieve the same rate until 1983, according to the Economic Council of Canada. The result, of course, is familiar to this
Family Allowances
House and country-it is continuing rising unemployment, continuing inflation, and an economy that has not kept pace with government expenditures. It seems to me that this government has a penchant for dividing a pie that keeps getting smaller and smaller and smaller, and it is the poor who suffer.
One of the first things the government did in 1965 when it declared its war on poverty was to set up a special planning secretariat within the PMO, and one of the first agencies to get the axe in the austerity program that followed was that special planning secretariat. It is the innocent who seem to have to bear the burden and the consequences of mismanagement of the economy by this government. The gap widened, notwithstanding studies such as that of Senator Croll, the various agencies, and the ministers of national health and welfare who come and go, show their concern, then leave the portfolio as they found it without any significant change as far as achieving the objective is concerned.
Most economic commentators, even the Minister of Finance, agree that the potential rate of real growth in Canada is about 5 per cent. At least for the rest of this decade, and possibly for the next five years, the rate of unemployment will not fall unless economic growth approaches 5 per cent. If the potential is 5 per cent, then the Canadian economy has not achieved sustained steady economic growth in recent years, nor is it likely to do so in the future. Since 1971, and including 1978, economic growth has exceeded 5 per cent only twice, almost achieved it once, and has been well below it four times. That record is hardly indicative of the kind of sustained steady economic growth referred to by Senator Croll as being necessary to eliminate poverty in Canada.
I have great regard for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), Mr. Speaker. I had regard and respect, although not to the same degree, for her predecessor. We heard him speak in the House when he introduced the bill that is now being amended, and we heard that the indexing of family allowances was going to solve some of the problems of inflation. It was a commendable move, one that received and has continued to receive the support of the House and the country. I have made the point over and over again in this House, however, that the major reason for indexation, as far as the working poor are concerned, is the fact that it is based on the consumer price index which does not give sufficient weight to food, shelter, and clothing. For the poor, eating out is academic; for them, sirloin steak is an unachievable luxury.
Let us examine the cumulative effect of indexing since 1974. In 1974 the rate of inflation was 10.4 per cent at a time when food prices rose by 16.3 per cent. Coincidentally, figures released yesterday by the Anti-Inflation Board show that food prices are currently running at 16.5 per cent this year. During those four years indexation meant an increase of 28.4 per cent in family allowances, whereas during the same period food prices increased by 46.1 per cent, which is the equivalent of the total increase in the consumer price index. Low income families continued to fall behind; the bill before the House is a painful admission of that fact.

October 31, 1978
Family Allowances
One would think that as a result of the more generous use of the Family Allowances Act, indexation which I have just referred to, introduced at about the same time, and a more comprehensive, generous unemployment insurance program, low income families would be able to catch up. But, sir, the reverse is true. They have in fact fallen behind.
Just a few days ago in this House the Economic Council of Canada tabled its fifteenth annual review and they made reference to the fact that in spite of a generous universal family and youth allowance program-I am paraphrasing- and the revised unemployment insurance program, the poor of this country in terms of government social transfer programs are falling behind. 1 quote from the Economic Council of Canada "A Time for Reason", fifteenth annual review, at page 93:
The combined effect of these and other changes was to increase the share of transfer payments going to members of the labour force and their families from 58 to 63 per cent, and the share going to those with some unemployment from 23 to over 30 per cent. The result has been a reinforcement of the incomes of the non-poor. Over all, the percentage of total government transfer directed towards family units with incomes below the poverty line dropped from 45 per cent to about 29 per cent.
The poor continue to fall behind. This government continues to react with ad hoc measures, which in the economic context of the day are not satisfactory and will not in fact achieve their objective.
Poverty, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare well knows, is everywhere. It is not confined to the so-called have-not provinces, one of which I have the honour to represent in this House, and it is not confined to any region. It is in our small towns and it is equally in our large cities. It is to be found in the rural parts of our country, and, of course, it is to be found in great measure in the northern areas and among our native peoples. It is something in this country which we measure in millions. Indeed, nobody will dispute the fact that given the measurement of poverty by Statistics Canada we have fully one-fifth of our population living well below the poverty line. This is something, sir, of which we should be ashamed.
A few days ago the Anglican Church of Canada tabled a report of a special task force on poverty in Canada. I quote from that report. They refer to the fact that:
Roughly one in six Canadians live in poverty. Almost two-thirds of the poor families in Canada belong to the 'working poor', that is, their heads participate in the work force, and work for annual incomes that are often less than they could receive as welfare clients.
That is something we often lose sight of in this House as we talk about unemployment insurance and about the number of people who are unemployed, that is, the plight of the working poor. I have them in my constituency, and I suspect they are in every constituency in the country.
This report goes on to say:
Of the remainder, who depend on the welfare system, 84 per cent do so because they are not capable of earning a living: the disabled, the female heads of young families-
Here is a group, growing, and continuing to fall further and further behind. You talk about equality in this country! It is a joke when one considers what is happening to female heads of families by comparison to their male counterparts.
I continue to quote:
Poverty is concentrated in certain areas, occupations, and educational levels. In the Atlantic provinces, 45 per cent of all families live in poverty; as do 46 per cent of all rural families across Canada. The incidence of poverty is well over 50 per cent in the case of farm workers, loggers, fishermen, trappers and hunters. 89 per cent of low-income families are headed by persons who have not completed high school.
We are talking about the poor in this country, the working poor, or the unemployed, or those who have to get by on fixed incomes. We dealt with this the other day when we were dealing with a bill amending the Old Age Security Act and increasing the amount payable under the guaranteed income supplement. We think of what inflation must mean to them. We think of food prices which have gone up this year so far by 16.5 per cent, shelter prices, the cost of heating a home, the cost of clothing and the cost to the female parent trying to provide an adequately nutrious diet for her family.
I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare: What happended to the Nutrition Canada survey? That was something undertaken by her predecessor. It was a very commendable move at the time when he was minister of national health and welfare. He is now Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde). That survey was completed, it was national in scope and it cost a considerable amount of money. It identified the problem in so far as the poor are concerned. It also indentified that we have serious nutritional problems in so far as middle income earners are concerned, large families, children going to school without an adequately nutritious breakfast, the situation where both parents are working and where the children cannot be given an adequate breakfast, where there is no adequate lunch preparation and they get by on junk food, soda pop, potato chips, and things that have no nutritional value. All too often when these children get to the first meal of the day it is around seven o'clock, because they have to wait for both parents to return home.
The minister's department made a submission to the Senate committee on poverty with respect to nutrition. It is worth noting because it refers to the impact that nutrition has on poor people. It refers to the impact it has on the learning ability of children, mental illness, and retardation. In fact the whole complex nature of the growing child is adversely affected by inadequate nutrition. That submission was made in 1971 to the senate committee on poverty, and we have heard nothing about it since.
If a poor family cannot maintain a child, and has to surrender the child to foster care, and this is a sad commentary, the government must provide the foster parent with two or more times the welfare allowance, plus the family allowance to care for the child.
I do not quarrel with what the minister is trying to do. I merely say to her that in the context of what this government

October 31, 1978

is doing, by the economic mess we are in today, it is the poor, the voiceless poor of this country who have to bear the greatest burden, whether it is with respect to inflation, or the consequences of government mismanagement, unemployment, regional disparity, or any of the problems that flow from the kind of situation that we find ourselves in today.
The number of families in Canada that are below the poverty line continues to grow at an alarming rate. I referred to the number of families with female heads living below the poverty line. In 1969, 41 per cent of the families with a female head were below the poverty line. In 1976 that figure had grown to 43.2 per cent. Last year, 1977, 44.1 per cent of families with a female head in this country were forced to live below the poverty line. The number of families living below the poverty line in Canada jumped by 10 per cent in 1977.
These figures are startling. If they are not, they should be. The number jumped from 645,000 in 1976 to 712,000 last year. The total number of Canadians living in poverty in Canada last year grew by over 300,000. Is it any wonder that we should concern ourselves with a bill of this nature?
I could talk about what the government is trying to do with regard to negative income tax. We will be going into committee of the whole. There will be ample opportunity to discuss those parts of this bill which cause some of us some problem. The confidentiality of the Income Tax Act, for example, is being breached in a very significant way by this bill. We will have more to say about that when we get into committee of the whole.
In order to arrive at a figure for family income, it is necessary to know the income of the other spouse. However, giving the minister the power to furnish information on the income of one spouse to another would be and is, as I have said, a very significant development.
Hon. members have anticipated what the Minister of National Health and Welfare would say. What would a Conservative government do? What would the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) do if he were the Prime Minister of Canada, and that will be his responsibility in a very short time?

The income tax structure is such that at the higher levels just about every change made in the Income Tax Act results in more money for a fortunate few. It is not a new result of Liberal social policy to make the middle income groups pay for benefits granted to those at the lower levels, and it is for this reason I feel strongly that the legislation should be studied further. speechtext:
that Bill C-203, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is an amending bill. It is very simple in form. It consists of two clauses. It seeks to delete from the Income Tax Act two subsections of section 234. It calls for its provisions to be retroactive to January 1, 1977, when subsections (5) and (6) came into force.
This bill appears for the second time on the order paper, it having appeared early in the last session when I put it on. This bill arises by reason of the fact that the guillotine was used in passing Bill C-22 in 1976. That bill was an income tax amendment bill arising out of the budget delivered previously, and this provision was one of those little provisions which was sneaked in. It is purely bureaucratic policy. It has nothing to do with government policy except to this extent: in the period since 1964 when the concept of the social insurance number was introduced the concept has been moving step by step toward a total identity card, and a total requirement for an identity card.
The way the social insurance number is applied is very unfair. It is fortunate in one way, and yet unfortunate that this House got to clause 65 of Bill C-22 when the guillotine fell, but when clause 75, which contained subsections (5) and (6) of section 234, came along, there was no question of any debate or discussion. However, fortunately some of us here who were aware of what was happening called out "on division", and so therefore we are not hemming and hawing when I present this bill.
What do subsections (5) and (6) of section 234 of the Income Tax Act provide? I will read them as follows:

October 31, 1978
Income Tax Act
(5)	Where an amount is to be paid or credited to a resident of Canada who is an individual, other than a trust, in circumstances where an ownership certificate referred to in subsection (1) is required to be completed, and the ownership certificate does not contain a social insurance number assigned to the individual by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the debtor or other person paying or crediting the amount shall deduct or withhold therefrom an amount equal to 25 per cent thereof and shall forthwith remit that amount to the Receiver General of Canada on account of the individual's tax for the year under Part I and shall submit therewith a statement in prescribed form,
(6)	Where an amount has been deducted or withheld under subsection (5) from an amount paid or credited to an individual, it shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to have been received by the individual at the time the amount was paid or credited to him.
That has certain implications too. My colleague, the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis), told me today about a constituent of his who is a mother of a young child who some years ago was given a $50 Canada Savings Bond. The bond matured this year. The mother went to a bank or trust company to cash the Canada Saving Bond. The child does not have a social insurance number, and it cannot qualify for one. The mother does not have one either. Why should she? She does not seek unemployment insurance. She does not have to be registered. However, the bank or trust company held back $12.50, to be credited to whom, the child, who is not a taxpayer, or to the mother, who is not a taxpayer? If the bond is cashed, 25 per cent of the face value and of the coupons can be claimed back only in the following taxation year. In the meantime, the government will have had the benefit of the funds. The individual concerned has been denied the value of the Canada Savings Bond which was sold by the government.
Whenever anyone bought a bond, he was told that he would be entitled to the face value at the sale of the bond. Now there is talk about a social insurance number, but millions and millions of bonds are outstanding. Incidentally, over four million people here in Canada do not have social insurance numbers, nor do they need them. Children and young married women who do not work have not applied for social insurance numbers. They are nowhere near being in a position where they might want to apply to either for Canada Pension or old age security.
Social insurance numbers were introduced in the first place so that people could get social security at age 65. Let us go back to the days of Mr. Pearson, who introduced the concept. He was questioned by the then leader of the opposition, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I have the quotations here. It was categorically asserted by the then prime minister that social insurance numbers would not be used for income tax purposes, but here we have the introduction of a use of the social insurance number attached to a penalty. There is now a requirement. Every T-l or T-l short form filed by personal taxpayers has a space for the social insurance number, but there is no penalty faced by taxpayers filing returns because none is provided. Taxpayers need not be registered for social insurance. There is no law which says that an individual has to be registered. Many of the wives of hon. members do not work and never have, that is outside, in order to qualify for unemployment insurance.

People must have social insurance numbers for purposes of unemployment insurance, but that is a social security purpose. However, millions of people in this country have not worked under those circumstances, and they can file income tax returns without having social security numbers. But now we have this amendment to the act which says that if a person cashes a Canada Savings Bond and that person is not the possessor of a social security number, the bank, trust company or other cashing agency shall deduct 25 per cent. There is no deduction from accumulated interest, but in some cases 25 per cent of the capital is sequestered. That is sheer confiscation, and I say it is unjust.
It was put forward by bureaucrats in the Department of National Revenue and, by God, they would never have got by me if I had been that department's parliamentary secretary, as I was in the past. I can assure you that, if you are a good parliamentary secretary, you ensure that that sort of thing stops when budget books are being prepared. At that time budgets were brought down in the early spring, so therefore budget books were prepared in the early winter months when proposals were put forward from all sides and considered by the interdepartmental committee on finance and national revenue, and other interested persons were called upon to discuss any particular proposal.
[DOT] (UI2)
This looks fine administratively, but I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the more use is made of the social security number, the more cheating there will be. It is rather strange, but when my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Big-gar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) raised a question the other day, I must confess that I was deeply disappointed in the answer given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who has become completely the tool of the bureaucracy when it comes to expressing views with regard to the use of the social security number, and likely her parliamentary secretary is too.
This gave rise to some newspaper articles. I will only refer to one in the Globe and Mail and one in the Gazette which appeared today indicating how far the use of the social security card has crept in by agencies which have no blessed business using it, particularly now that there are computers which store and compare data. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said that with a program of millions of dollars she had to have a computer so as to prevent cheating. Has she seen the statistics on the types of cases involving cheating of unemployment insurance, such as cases of people holding 50 or 60 cards? Why is that? Because with the insistence on the social security number, the value of the card increases, and greater and greater reliance is placed upon it as the true means of identification. Then it becomes an absolute sinecure to cheat the UIC in any manner that can be devised.
Certainly today trust companies do not ask the holder of Canada Savings Bonds whether they may see his social security card or the ownership certificate or that the redemption form be filled out. So long as there is a nine digit number that is reasonable for the area, they say, "Thank you very much,
October 31, 1978

madam, that is perfectly fine". It does not mean a thing because, for the purpose of the Income Tax Act, this is supposed to be a cross check. Someone might have Canada Savings Bonds which they should not have, and they are trying to cheat.
I do not know what promoted this because we were not able to question the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on the reasoning for it, but all I say is that this is a nefarious subsection in the Income Tax Act. I do not know whether members in the House have considered how unjust it is when, in other cases, they say there is a withholding of 25 per cent of the dividends to a foreign owner, or income which you are paying to a former resident and you withhold 25 per cent in order to ensure that your money is covered for a potential income tax. But it is not that, it is 25 per cent of the capital value as well. Therefore, the Department of Finance is lying in its teeth to the public of Canada when it says that people will be repaid the face value of the Canada Savings Bonds they purchase. Now they have added this kicker, "provided you have a social insurance number." That was not a condition of the purchase of those bonds.
Very few bonds that were subject to this condition are being presented for cashing now. This bill only came into force in
1976.	As a matter of fact, it became effective on January 1,

I would like to make one last point on this. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that there are many senior citizens in Canada who drew their old age pension before 1964, before there was a requirement for a social insurance number, and they have never had to file for one? There has to be a marriage certificate, and then something like secondary identification or a tax notice on which a person's name has appeared, or some such silly thing. You ask elderly persons of 85 or 86 to go through this rigamarole to get a social insurance number so that they are able to cash in their savings without having 25 per cent of them confiscated, until they can file an income tax return in the following year, which they are not required to do any way!
