Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to spend a few minutes making
Income Tax Act
some comments on Bill C-203 proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I will preface my remarks by saying that I do not in any way profess to be an authority on the tax system or to have the kind of legislative background that the hon. member for Edmonton West has, but having read the bill and after listening to him, I thought I might offer a few comments.
I was perplexed as to the reason why he was so exercised by the subject matter of the bill. I noticed the outpouring of emotion, and it seemed to me rather odd because in my constituency, for instance, the minor hockey league requires that all children have social insurance numbers before being allowed to play on any of the teams which represent the municipality outside that area, and so do indeed some of the other minor leagues, even for house league play, as do some schools for their records. So it seems to me that if this is acceptable, it is not because those organizations have any legislative authority to enforce it, other than to bring some pressure to bear on both the parents and the children who may or may not be able to play in those leagues.
But when we are dealing with a measure which is designed to improve the efficiency of the tax system, I have some difficulty in understanding the hon. member's indignation. During oral questions hon. members opposite have indicated with great moral indignation that apparently the efficiency of government is not as high as it should be. They have asked what ministers are going to improve administrative procedures, so that money can be recovered or at least not lost. If it is acceptable to parents and a large number of other people to have social insurance numbers for minor league sport, it seems somewhat peculiar that such a requirement in the Income Tax Act to improve its efficiency would be wrong.
I should like to respond to some of the points raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West. When social insurance numbers were introduced in 1964 by the previous prime minister, the government of the day made commitments regarding the new system. The commitment made was that information contained in application forms for social insurance numbers would be processed and maintained in Ottawa for government purposes, including unemployment insurance and the then proposed Canada Pension Plan. A further commitment was made that the confidentiality of this information would be protected.
No commitment was made then, or at any other time, to the effect that social insurance numbers would not be used in order to identify individuals for the purposes of a common system of government record keeping, such as that recommended by the Glassco commission. The hon. member indicated that the present minister had violated an undertaking by a previous government and prime minister. Perhaps that is not in accordance with the facts. The confidentiality of material on application forms is guarded very carefully. At that time it was stated that the information would be used for unemployment insurance, the Canada Pension Plan and other social measures,

October 31, 1978
Income Tax Act
but no commitment was made that it would not be used as an extension into the common system of government record keeping.
The introduction into the Income Tax Act of the provision for withholding tax respecting ownership certificates which do not bear individual social insurance numbers does not make it mandatory for any taxpayer to produce his social insurance number, or indeed, to acquire one if he has not previously applied for the assignment of a social insurance number because of some provision in the law. If a person chooses not to apply for a social insurance number, and for some reason feels it would be uncomfortable to have one, because of some moral objection against it, there is no requirement that he must. As I understand it, the law requires that 25 per cent of the interest coupon value would be prepaid. It would be credited to the tax system, and it would be refundable if no other tax was owing.
Also I wonder if the hon. member for Edmonton West was correct when he suggested that 25 per cent of the face value of bonds would have to be deposited. I question that. Perhaps I am not the financier the hon. member is, but my understanding is that it would be the coupon value. I am sure the hon. member would agree that the principal of the bond is not taxable, but the coupon value is. In fact the current issue of Canada Savings Bonds do not have coupons attached to them. Much of what he raised in his argument will disappear as we go forward.
At this point in time, I question that there are four million Canadians who do not have social insurance numbers. Obviously that number will decline dramatically if substantial numbers of school children are required to have social insurance numbers for school and minor sports purposes. The most commonly purchased bonds in Canada are Canada Savings Bonds. If those bonds do not have coupons, the use of this procedure would be considerably less.
I hope the hon. member was not implying in his remarks that the 25 per cent was a penalty. It is a clear requirement to prepay in order to have on record that a certain amount of money was cashed. Further, there is a liability on the part of the person who cashed the bond to prepay an amount to his income tax account, not forfeit it. The hon. member referred to one inequity in a system where money is credited to the account of a taxpayer. If there is a refund owing to that taxpayer, that money may be in the system for a period up to a year. I suppose it could be argued that essentially there would be no interest rate, whereas if the money went to the taxpayer it could be reinvested or used for some other purpose. That is the narrow aspect of it, in terms of people cashing bond interest and not being in the category of owing some type of income tax.
The alternative to the existing social insurance number requirement would be the withholding of tax on all payments of interest. Recently the United States Treasury proposed a mandatory withholding on all interest because of the extent of under-reporting of income in this category by taxpayers in the United States. While this would resolve the compliance problem, it would cause some hardship for a large number of

taxpayers. This should be considered only if experience reveals that existing procedures are inadequate.
I apologize to the House and the proposer of the bill that I did not have time to do the amount of research I would like to in terms of an estimate regarding the amount of bond interest not reported. I think in some cases non-compliance with the act is fairly significant. It was rather interesting that an hon. member opposite would set out his argument in great flowing terms that we should not use modern methods to increase the efficiency of the tax system, and therefore perhaps operate the system less inefficiently. Surely any hon. member who has listened to questions directed to ministers involved in social programs, finance, employment or manpower programs, will realize the theme of the questions was efficiency of administration. If the opposition is sincere and believes what it proposes in question form, then such an argument is not terribly consistent.
I am not aware of income reporting slips being issued for bank interest, or any other type of investment, without social insurance numbers being included on them. Some tax forms without social insurance numbers are mailed to elderly senior citizens who have never had such numbers allocated to them. But I am sure approximately 90 per cent of all income tax forms mailed to taxpayers include social insurance numbers.
I find it a little bit strange that in an effort to improve the efficiency of the tax system the hon. member for Edmonton West would argue so vigorously against a practice that is accepted apparently in minor sports, in schools, in all the business transactions involving every other type of investment and, indeed, I would venture to think in well over 90 per cent of all the income tax forms filed in Canada in any one year.
Those are the comments I wanted to make, and for the reasons I have given, 1 would find it very difficult to support Bill C-203.

It seems to me that it would have been more realistic, fairer and no more complicated than necessary to ask the banks and the financial institutions where savings bond interest coupons are cashed in to give an application form to their customers who do not have a social insurance number and to urge these customers to complete these forms for future use. It seems to me that this decision was made rather arbitrarily and with no period of transition. I have in my office an employee who used to work for a Canadian chartered bank. Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks I made in the debate on second reading of Bill C-10 just before five o'clock, I tried to make the point that there are some aspects of it which I think should be studied further. If my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) looked a bit worried and wondered where I was proceeding in light of what I was saying, I would like to tell her that my purpose was to try to make her realize that this bill is not perfect.
This bill launches out in a new area by using the Income Tax Act not only for the purpose of collecting taxes from Canadians, but for making payments out of income tax collections to those who need them. Although it is new in that it moves into that area and is therefore to be welcomed, no one knows better than the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the Income Tax Act is still full of many loopholes, many opportunities for the rich to profit. If those loopholes could have been plugged, she would not have had to agree to reducing the amount of the family allowance from $26 to $20 a month.
From time to time we have had a good deal to say about the unfairness of the Income Tax Act in terms of what it does for the wealthy. I have two or three statistics here that have been given on previous occasions by members of my party, and I think they make the point.
In 1972, there were 92 Canadians with incomes of $50,000 or more who paid no income tax. They managed to take advantage of the escape clauses and the loopholes in the legislation. In 1973 that number rose to 156. I point out that the situation is getting worse, because in 1974, the last year for which I have this kind of statistic, 252 persons in Canada with incomes of $50,000 or more paid no income tax whatsoever. The average income of those 252 persons was $92,000 and 17 of them made over $200,000.
It is because of that sort of situation in the Income Tax Act that I wish the Minister of National Revenue had had a little more influence with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). It is good what is happening in that a $200 refundable tax credit is being established. As I say, the Income Tax Act is not only being used to take money from persons, but to give money to certain people. A lot more money would be available for the equalization of incomes if the provisions of the Income Tax Act could be tightened up.
October 31, 1978

One of the discussions in which we take part around this place has to do with whether or not we are making progress. One of the persons who has documented very well the continuing discrepancy in the amount of income received is the Minister of National Health and Welfare herself. I would point out that according to Statistics Canada the distribution of income as between the bottom 20 per cent of income earners and the top 20 per cent has changed very little. In 1951 the bottom 20 per cent received 4.4 per cent of total income earned. The figure fluctuated a bit from 1951 to 1975 when it was down to 4 per cent. In 1976, it was 4.1 per cent. So it may be said, as was said by a member at the foot of the government side the other day, that in terms of dollars the poor now have more than they used to have. But in terms of their percentage of the national pie, they have scarcely moved at all. On the other hand, as opposed to the fact that the bottom 20 per cent received about 4 per cent of the earned income, the top 20 per cent got around 42.8 per cent-the figure went up and down a bit-and in the last year for which I have statistics their share was around 43 per cent.
It is this I had in mind when in the few minutes for which I spoke before five o'clock I said that for all the good there was in the bill now before us there was room for a completely new look at the income tax legislation. I realize this bill is in the name of the Minister of Finance and that I seem to be speaking about it as though it belonged to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I feel it is more hers than his though, because it does deal with a change in the way in which family allowances are provided.
The other day in the course of another speech I was making, the Minister of National Health and Welfare made an interjection which I did not hear at the time but which I enjoyed very much when I got to the Hansard office and read what she had said. I had suggested that if she made certain improvements in the old age pension she would improve the stock of the Liberal party at the next election and might even become leader of the Liberal party. Her interjection, which I did not hear but which was on the record, was: "Minister of Finance would be okay." In light of the statements she has been making in speeches around the country, and in light of what she has said about loopholes in the Income Tax Act to which I have referred tonight, I would be quite happy if she got that portfolio and pushed to the limit the possibilities there are for equalizing the distribution of income by making changes in the Income Tax Act.
In saying, as I did a moment ago, that if the Income Tax Act were applied on a fair and equitable basis there would be sufficient money for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to have instituted a $200 cash credit without cutting back on the basic amount of the family allowance payments, 1 implied, and I hope the implication was clear, that in our view this is what ought to have been done. We approve the refundable tax credit idea; it is one we have proclaimed from this part of the House for a long time. But we do not think it is necessary to reduce the basic amount from $26 to $20.
Family Allowances
I am aware of all the arguments about people in the middle and upper brackets not needing the money, but I believe many families will notice the difference, especially in the face of rising prices, when they are confronted with this reduction of $6 per child, especially families whose incomes are such that they will not get the $200 tax credit in March or April. We know the reason the minister could not get through the kind of program we would like to see. It was because of the inequities and loopholes that are still present in the Income Tax Act.
Having said all that as an indication of our attitude toward Bill C-10, I should like to say a few things about elements in this measure of which we approve. We note with respect to the family allowances program that universality is being maintained. It is true that the amount everyone will get is reduced, but the program is still to be applied universally. That is the way it was brought in in the first place and that is the form in which it has survived over the years.
There was a time in the parliament of 1968-72 when the government tried to bring in a program bearing the name FISP. It almost got approved but the measure died on the order paper as that parliament ended. The result of the program would have been to destroy the universality of family allowance payments. In the succeeding parliament when the government was in a minority position FISP was thrown out the window and universality was maintained. Despite any shortcomings the bill before us may have, it is continuing the principle of universality and we welcome that.
We welcome also the fact that the principle of indexation is still alive. It may not be well this year, or in 1979, but it is still alive. The basic amount of the family allowance will be cut back in January from $26 to $20 a month, but in 1980 it will be escalated or indexed according to the rise in the cost of living.
It is also a fact that the $200 tax credit is to be indexed annually and that the $18,000 cut-off is to be indexed. I am glad to see the minister nodding her head to confirm that the things I am saying are true. What worries me about this assurance that indexation will continue is that this minister may not always be in her present portfolio and that under another minister it may have less value. We remember how the indexation of family allowances was suspended for a year-the government cancelled it-and now it is being cut back for the second time. So who can be sure that the guarantee of indexing in 1980 or 1981 will be honoured when the time comes? Nevertheless, if there are enough of us here who believe in these things, let us hope universality of social payments and the right of indexation will survive.
I am looking forward to the speech the Minister of National Health and Welfare is going to make tonight, and I hope she will take the same stand with regard to the indexing of family allowances that she took the other day with regard to the indexing of benefits under the Old Age Security Act. If we can have that kind of assurance from her, well, we will have to

Family Allowances
count on it, but down the road I suspect that these things will still have to be fought for time and time again.
That is something I have learned from experience around this place. No battle ever really stays won. I remember how long and hard we fought to get rid of the means test and to get pensions on a universal basis and when it happened there was really great rejoicing and satisfaction, but after only a decade, or a generation at most, some people were talking about the means test as though it was something that might be employed again.
I am conscious of the long battle we have waged to get the government into our economy for the benefit of all the people the government represents. I am conscious of those years when we were aware of how little the private sector and the free enterprise economy did for our people, but today, when we have many government programs which have made life better in Canada, "privatizing" has become a word which both Liberals and Tories like to mouth in this place. We are aware of the fact that battles which have been won have to continue to be fought.
I welcome the battle that the Minister of National Health and Welfare fought inside the cabinet, even at a time of restraint and cutbacks, not to have a total cutback in the family allowance but to get the kind of program we have before us tonight. It is a fact that although people in the higher middle and upper income brackets will be receiving fewer dollars for their children in that they will get only a $20 a month family allowance, in the case of those where the family income is $18,000 or less there will be, in return for that $6 a month they will lose, a $200 credit in March or April of the succeeding year. That is good. We welcome that, but we think that the principles underlying it must not be forgotten.
We think also that this beginning of the use of the Income Tax Act to make payments to people should be pushed a long way, and the way to push it is to plug some of the loopholes which make it possible, as I have already said, for 252 people in 1974 to make $50,000 a year or more and 17 of them over $200,000 but not pay one cent of income tax. We are reminded of all the various escape clauses there are. If ever a sentence in the Bible was true, it is that one about things being given to those who already have. The income tax seems to be very biblical in that respect.
Before I sit down, and because the Minister of National Health and Welfare is on the list to speak, there are one or two points I hope she might deal with when she gets the floor. I wonder if she will be able to tell us of any discussions she has had with the provinces about these matters. I have two points in mind. On the one hand, when persons have their allowance cut from $26 to $20, does the minister know whether any provinces are likely to make up the difference?
The other side of the story relates to the $200. What is going to happen in March or April of next year when some families get $200 per child? In some cases that will amount to a total of $600 or $800. What will that do to the position of those families which are on welfare or benefiting from any social program in any of the provinces? I realize that this is

totally federal legislation, but still there is hardly anything left in this country which does not become the subject of discussion between Ottawa and the provinces.
Then there is one other matter which I hope the minister will have something to say about tonight. I believe reference was made to it this afternoon. 1 refer to the consumer price index. I welcome the fact that the minister has stood firm and won the continuation of indexation of family allowances as well as pensions, but the recently announced change in the way the consumer price index is made up gives some of us cause for concern. I refer in particular to the downgrading of food as an element in the basket, particularly at a time when Statistics Canada tells us that the cost of food is rising. I believe this month it rose more than in any month for a very long time.
This will affect pensioners and those who depend heavily on family allowances very severely. There is already the feeling, if not the fact, that indexing is always behind and never seems to keep up with rising costs, but if the consumer price index is being revised in a way which will result in even less accurate increases under indexation, that is something which is very serious.
I do not recall whether I have had discussions with this minister during the time she has been in this portfolio on this issue, but certainly 1 have discussed it with previous ministers of national health and welfare. I refer to the desirability of having a special index for senior citizens or for families. After all, the consumer price index is made up by Statistics Canada on the basis of the Canadian population as a whole, but senior citizens have special needs on which they spend their money, and mothers of families, especially those who are having a difficult time, also have special needs. I realize that the consumer price index is tabulated under the aegies of another minister-it does not come under this minister-but as I recall, at least some of her predecessors have expressed an interest in looking at this, and I wonder if she will tell us whether she has tried to get Statistics Canada to come up with an index which would be appropriate to those who depend on family allowances and to those who are in receipt of old age pensions.
Those are our views respecting this bill. As we have said several times, it is good that in this time of restraint, which we think is false, uneconomic and turning the country the wrong way, one minister has been able to bring about some progress, and in that sense we welcome this bill. It will have our support, but we shall keep on pressing for the changes which ought to be made in the Income Tax Act to get rid of those loopholes so there will not be so much leakage and there will be more money for distribution to those who need it, whether we are talking about senior citizens or about families.
We are also glad that provision is being made for the $200 per child to be given to mothers in the spring. We will go along with the technical arrangements which are necessary to make that possible. We heard some explanation of that this afternoon from the Minister of Finance, and I look forward to hearing from the Minister of National Health and Welfare tonight. I hope she will deal with some of the points I have

raised, and I hope she might even go so far as to make the commitment that, if she ever does become Minister of Finance, she will do something about the gross inequities in the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues, I am pleased to participate in this debate.
We are now studying a bill to reduce from $25 to $20 the family allowances paid for every child. This bill also proposes to grant a tax credit of up to $200 for every child in families whose income does not exceed $18,000 a year. In addition, any family with earnings of up to $46,000 a year and at least seven children under 18 years of age could also claim tax credits to be indexed annually, according to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
That new program is, of course, a positive step towards the redistribution of wealth among the middle class who are always the first to bear the brunt of the economic problems we have had to face in the last decade. Through this new system of tax credits, we are getting away from the situation where family allowances existed for all families. Their purpose was to encourage demographic progress in the country and, in addition, to give substantial financial assistance to large families.
Naturally, with the new system based on the redistribution of wealth, many families will lose that financial aid. In addition, the new measures, which the people do not understand too well, will surely create a nightmare for our bureaucracy. Let us just imagine, Mr. Speaker, all the confusion that will arise in the income tax returns. Many interested parties have pointed out that millions of women who have no income, and consequently do not file income tax returns, will now have to change their habits.
It also appears that everyone qualifying for tax credits will have to file a separate income tax form, which means that in a single income family where the breadwinner is the father or the husband, the wife or mother will have to send in her own income tax form. And what about the problems of separated couples and the incomes of dependent children? It looks like it is going to be an absolute administrative mess. Revenue Canada will have to check over two million additional income tax forms, make sure that all statements filed by husbands and wives agree, scrutinize all enclosures, income adjustments and required documents.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy I do no work in the Department of National Revenue because I am sure several people in that department will have a big headache next spring. I also expect a full scale publicity campaign will be necessary to inform the public about these changes. All in all, I think I would rather work in a publicity agency than in the Department of National Revenue. Maybe these agencies will pull the big buck out of this mess.
Family Allowances
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that benefits from family allowances decrease as income goes up since they are taxable. The tax credit granted until now, $50 for each child, does not help the poorest families since they do not pay income tax nor the more affluent ones since they can accumulate that credit in the form of a tax rebate not exceeding $500.
We must not forget that families in the poorest category depend upon family allowances as a substantial source of income and that with these new provisions they will now be forced to wait for the payment of the tax credit which will be paid, presumably only once a year. The tax credit will not be paid automatically, as it is now. That will therefore result in the poorest families being even more dependent upon provincial social welfare, thus increasing the provincial burden in that area. So the cost of providing for our children will no longer be used as criterion, but the family income level will.
I think the proposed provisions are somewhat premature because their consequences have not been cleared up. This measure has been widely criticized because of the difficulty to. implement the system and of the administrative costs which will be incurred. Also, we should not forget that those funds come from the unemployment insurance cuts which were announced and which will deprive some 250,000 to 300,000 unemployed of the benefits.
Mr. Speaker, on September 14, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said in a speech in St. John's, Newfoundland, and I quote:
It should be clearly understood that these benefits are directed towards those people who have immediate needs.
Mr. Speaker, I am terribly surprised because if the government is really aware of the fact that the needs of many persons and families who find it terribly difficult to make both ends meet are immediate, why did they change the family allowances program so that those families will have to wait for one whole year before receiving the new tax credits?
In the same speech, the minister added the following, I quote:
Finally, we must define the new measures in light of our economy; the formula should encourage people to work and stimulate our productivity.
Mr. Speaker, can the minister tell us how we can encourage somebody to work when we have the highest unemployment rate ever seen and when our economy is very weak? Why this relentlessness to make a scapegoat of the small earner?
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I must establish clearly that the bill before us is creating a certain ambiguity with respect to the term "family income". On what criteria is it determined? On the income of one spouse, of both spouses, of both spouses and their children, of separated or divorced spouses? I think this point should be clarified. Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to speak tonight in this House of what I also believe to be the most fundamental reform, and I would like to correct the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who suggested this afternoon that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was exaggerating when he said this afternoon, in introducing his bill, that this was a most important reform. He did not say that it was the only reform undertaken by the government in the last ten years, but rather that it was the most significant social policy reform that this House had seen in at least ten years, if not more.
This reform is directed towards Canadian children. It appears to me most important and appropriate that we study this legislation immediately after a bill which considerably increases our senior citizens' share of the national income. These are the two most vulnerable ages in periods when economic restraint must be imposed more strictly than we would want.
In Canada, in the year and two months since I have been responsible for the national health and welfare portfolio, I have noticed, and I think it is important to indicate this to the people of this country, that it is as easy to mobilize public opinion in favour of our senior citizens as it is difficult to mobilize the same public opinion over what should be done to ensure that the children of this country, who are the number one human resource of a nation, receive their rightful share in the government's social policies and income distribution schemes. I will say a few words about that later in dealing with two issues raised by the official critic of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), concerning the universality and the indexing of family allowances.
It is a great pleasure for me to speak, as a minister whose mandate is in part to ensure that poverty in Canada is eradicated, if at all possible, or at least decreased. This bill is in fact, let us not deny it, a redistribution proposal.
If one studies the bill proposed by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), one must face the fact that this project, which is the most fundamental reform in social policies of the last decade, basically is a project which touches upon redistribution. Therefore, it will hurt some Canadians and it will help others. Why did we do that, who are these people, and in what order of magnitude was the reform conducted, are questions which should be answered in the House tonight.

I should like to direct my attention to a few points made by the two opposition members who spoke this afternoon and tonight. If we speak of redistribution, we speak of poverty. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for St. John's East making a grand, general speech about poverty in Canada. His speech was full of wrong statistics. As he said, the Conservative party is against poverty. My party is against poverty, and so is every Canadian.

We have decided to correct some of the injustices of the socioeconomic system vis-a-vis families by adding to the basic universal family allowance a special new cheque, an annual one in the amount of $200 per child. That cheque will go to all families below a certain income. That is what we are proposing. In other words, we decided to put together the best of selectivity and universality.
The hon. member for St. John's East also mentioned that the number of poor in Canada had not decreased. That is not true. The social programs which were devised in the sixties have decreased the total number of poor in Canada. The total number has not been decreased enough, but there has been a consistent fight against poverty. He said that approximately 20 per cent of Canadians are poor. In order to correct the record, let me indicate that 20 per cent of Canadians share 4 per cent to 5 per cent of the wealth, but of that percentage, half of them are really poor.
If the hon. member wants to talk about poverty, he should refer to a few more of the facts rather than just generalities. He did not tell Canadians that it is not fashionable to talk about poverty today because there is no longer visible, flagrant poverty in Canada. People no longer really suffer from malnutrition as they did when I was a teacher 20 years ago. People no longer suffer from the effects of unacceptable housing conditions. Poverty is far more difficult to fight. It is far more difficult to sell to Canadians the fact that poverty should be put on the map of urgent problems to tackle because it has gone underground and has become less apparent.
The usual criteria used to define a certain neighbourhood or certains quarters of cities as being poor areas have changed. It is more difficult to use the usual criteria. The hon. member for St. John's East did not acknowledge that at all. He repeated that Canada was in an economic mess. We on this side believe in Canada. We do not believe Canada is in a mess at all. In the last ten years the income of the average Canadian has increased by 25 per cent. This is in constant dollars, which means that I am taking into account the inflation which has
October 31, 1978

existed over the years. Our wealth, incomes, the goods to which we have access have increased by 25 per cent, as evidenced by improvement in the physical environment of our homes. Increased standards have been passed on to everyone, including the poor in Canada. Their hopes and aspirations have naturally increased. If a list of the basic goods a poor family possesses today was produced by a social worker, it would be quite different from what it was in the past. I hope it would include such things as television sets. Of course, television sets would not have been included in such a list back in the sixties, because total wealth, hopes and aspirations were not at the level they are today.
Also the hon. member referred to the fifteenth report of the Economic Council of Canada. He quoted figures in an attempt to prove the total number of families living in poverty has increased tremendously. They have not increased, they have decreased, especially if we refer to statistics in proportion to the total population of Canada. I should like to refer to the fact that the incidence of poverty has declined from 1971 to 1975, the period referred to by the hon. member as the one in which poverty increased. That illustrates and provides us with points of reference when we talk of social policy and poverty in the country.
I should like to refer to the social policy budget of the government. Approximately 15 years ago, that budget was roughly 12 per cent of the total budget of the Canadian nation. The Department of National Defence received the biggest share of all federal government expenditures. The social portion of the national budget for 1978 amounts to 33 per cent. So when the hon. member says that the share which goes to people in need has decreased, that is not so. It has increased tremendously.
I would also remind the hon. member that if the total number of poor families and people on welfare decrease in Canada, of course the total number of welfare payments will decrease. Although the hon. member may have made his speech in good faith, his erroneous assertions regarding poverty do not demonstrate where the Conservative party stands regarding family allowances and child benefits.

So the comment about breach of confidentiality does not make much sense. If he wants to be technical and really maniacal about the sacrosanct confidentiality of the Income Tax Act, I can tell him there will be a one-page form included with the family allowance cheque in January which in most cases will go to mothers. This form can be filled out by the father or mother. If the father does not want to tell the mother how much he earns, she can sign the form and he can fill it in and send it. That should satisfy the breach of confidentiality charge. The hon. member must be surrounded by very wealthy people. In ordinary social classes, especially in poor families, people know what money they make. They also know what they make when they work on the weekend as waiters in hotel bars or whatever sideline it is they find to make ends meet. Everybody knows approximately what they make when they are poor. The hon. member is just raising a problem that does not exist for poor Canadians, those of whom we are speaking tonight.
My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked for my views on universality. I have already spoken on this earlier tonight. He also asked me about indexation. I regret that to create the bank of money needed to start the new annual cheque for mothers, we would have to add to the "pot" the indexation of 1979. That is really what we did. We put in that bank all the money we could because we knew Canadians would not agree to pay more taxes and that there was no other source of funds than shifting benefits within the existing system, making it more fair and equitable.
I regret that the indexation for this year has gone but I am very pleased that full indexation will be on the books for the new benefit, the ceiling at which a family can claim that benefit, and for the family allowance as well. I want to make it clear that indexation is provided for in the future.
Referring to the CPI, Mr. Speaker, and to a more proper measure of the increased cost of living, the only thing I can say tonight is that I will look into it and hope to be ready to answer questions during committee of the whole discussion. But I do not have anything to say that would help the debate at this point.
I should like to speak now of a few practical aspects of the new child tax credit. Some have said it is just unacceptable that the poor would suddenly get a huge sum of money once a year when they do not know how to spend $10. I am sure that is not true. I am not sure that mothers of good, wealthy families know how to spend money better than poor people.
Another fact about which I want to speak is the possible budgeting problem of families with an annual benefit versus several monthly benefits or benefits given through several instalments. I want to say to the House that this new benefit will use the tax machinery. This is the first time that the tax system will be used to deliver benefits to people. That is why we give it that funny name-the refundable child tax credit, although it is a cheque sent to mothers. It goes through the tax system and because of that this machinery has been set up only for annual deliveries. In future years it will be important to monitor what is best for, and what is wanted by, mothers.
October 31, 1978

In 1979 when the program is introduced it will work this way. In January a form will be sent to mothers along with the first reduced family allowance cheque. By the end of January all Canadian mothers will get $20 per child per month. Mothers in need, mothers on welfare, mothers in receipt of mothers' allowance, will, of course, be entitled to the new tax credit. It is they who will need it most and need it most urgently.
During January, February and March, the time at which the cheques will start being delivered to families, there will be a relative loss in the family allowances. For families in need with more than three children, this may be a practical problem but not for other families. This bothers me a great deal but there was no other way to introduce the system at a given point in time. So this is the loss we have to live with in order to gain much more.
The Minister of Finance gave the amount of these net gains. They are huge gains-gains for people in provinces as wealthy as Alberta, with its rapidly growing economy but where there are 43,000 poor families who will benefit from money that now goes to the richer families of Alberta and coming from all Canadian taxpayers, to the extent that about a $5 million net gain will go to Alberta in 1979. This takes into account the reductions in family allowances. This is very significant. In Ontario I think the reductions and the redistribution between families will offset each other. In other words, the poorer the provinces, the bigger the transfer payments, for we are now talking of the equivalent of a new transfer payment to individuals.
I was speaking of the real problem of family budgeting which may arise for the two first months of this year. 1 do not know of any solution to it. If hon. members have some solutions to suggest I would like to hear from them. As for the future, I do not foresee any problem because mothers will be receiving the $600 or $800 cheque. If they have three or four children, they can put aside a certain amount for monthly budgeting and spend whatever is needed for a down payment or repayment on a fridge, a washing machine or whatever might be needed in the home. Purchases like this ultimately benefit the children.
I acknowledge that problem and we will monitor it to see if the bill will need to be amended in the future or the idea of instalments introduced. We will be able to see what will be the most helpful to those in need. I say to hon. members, let the people concerned tell us what they want. I think it is important to listen to them. They are not well organized and their voices are not usually heard by politicians. Mothers of families are a segment of our society that is not represented by pressure groups. We do not know what they think or want.
It is important that the universality of family allowances be established once and for all.

In all honesty I think members on the other side could agree with me that family allowances, no matter the economic circumstances of a family, are a right, by which the government shows that the nation is responsible for the well-being of all children who, after all, are the best of all its natural resources. That right is not well established in Canadian philosophy, if I may use that word. I have travelled across the country many times. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) is always astonished when she discovers she is not the only one who talks to people. We all pretend to be close to people, and we try to be. It is important to discuss with various groups what Canadians want in terms of universality. Universality is established right now, but I point out to Canadians that family allowances, as a program of child benefits, are the weakest element of our social policy, I suggest, in the eyes of those who have economic interests to defend above and before all others. I say this to the House in order to assist and to raise the consciousness of my colleagues, and through television of the Canadian public, to ensure that we continue to see the merit of a universal family allowance. We will add whatever reforms are needed to be certain that in addition to the basic family allowance whatever is required for those in need will be available.
No doubt many other questions will arise. I will conclude by outlining what the prospect will look like for mothers in 1979. By the way, I am very pleased to say that mothers or fathers when they have legal custody of their child or children, will receive the cheque. It may seem strange to always refer to the status of women in this way, but for so many years women did not have their voices heard adequately in this House. I think that all hon. members will realize that every one of the provincial advisory councils on the status of women as well as the federal Advisory Council on the Status of Women recommended that the tax exemption for children be abolished and replaced with a tax credit. The federal Advisory Council on the Status of Women made it known publicly that it was very pleased with the new tax credit. A few other women's groups in Canada also approved of it, but I must admit that most women regretted the small cut we had to make in order to create the new program which, in the final analysis, is an important plus for all Canadian mothers in need, including mothers on welfare, and the Indian mothers who do not even exist as such under the Income Tax Act right now. It also means a great deal to the mothers of the poor families, in other words the working poor, who work but cannot make enough to live above the poverty line. Altogether it will mean an additional $300 million redistributed to Canadian families living below the poverty line, and this is worth quite a fight.

Just in case the minister did not have an opportunity to review some of the events of the past few years in this country, she might want to refresh herself with one committee that was appointed at the end of World War II. In fact, it was during the period of the war at a time when the participation of women in the work force had increased very rapidly, for obvious reasons. In 1939, just prior to World War II, 24.4 per cent of the work force was women. By the end of 1945 it had risen to 33.2 per cent. However, within a period of one year the work force dropped back to 25.3 per cent.
A subcommittee was appointed called the advisory committee on reconstruction, post-war problems of women. It had to do with this very question of the rapid increase of the number of women in the work force and what was likely to take place with respect to their continued employment. Interestingly enough, one of the members of that committee was later a New Democratic Party member of parliament, Grace Maclnnis.
The report said very clearly that some steps would have to be taken with regard to the training programs and unemployment insurance benefits. Interestingly enough, a recommendation was made in terms of a family allowance program. I quote from one of the recommendations of the subcommittee:
It was felt that the addition to the family income from children's allowances paid to the mother and by her spent for the welfare of her children may well be an alleviating factor in the mental attitude which may result from the surrender of the double income.
This scheme obviously was to work as an incentive to create more opportunity for some women to provide household care for children under certain kinds of informal day care programs, and for other women who had decided to participate more fully in the paid work force to continue to do so.
The sad fact is that through the introduction of those child care benefits more than 30 years ago, the participation rate dropped in one year from 33.2 per cent to 25.3 per cent. None are so deaf and dumb as those who refuse to learn from the lessons of history.
If the minister does not think that this initiative which she herself describes as being revolutionary today is not going to create a very serious situation for many thousands of presently employed women, she should give very long serious and sober second thought to it. minister has built into this tax credit program could in fact create a very serious problem and growing hardship for a number of Canadian women.
In 1978, 48 per cent of all adult Canadian women were in the paid labour force. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), speaking to this House some months ago when presenting his budget, one of the immediate problems that confronts the Canadian economy today is the growing number of Canadian women who are working. I quote from his statement on the evening on which he presented his budget:
An important reason for the growth of our labour force has been the growing number of Canadian women who are working. Since 1970 the number of adult women in the labour force has increased from 1.9 million to 2.7 million, a rise of more than 40 per cent.
The Minister of Finance went on to point out that the surge of young people as well as the increased participation of women has created a problem. He did add on that occasion that this surge would not last as there was a growing number of empty desks in the classrooms. What the minister was saying in a kind of code language and what other ministers have said before and since is that there are too many women who want to work outside the home.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) asked in the House on October 17 if the government plans to pay grants in lieu of taxes in respect of its facilities outside the national capital region. He went on to inquire whether the government is examining the status of the property of the Fraser River harbour commission in Surrey, British Columbia.
The government's system of grants in lieu of taxes is a national system which applies in all parts of Canada, and not just within the national capital region as suggested. Payments on departmental property are made under the Municipal Grants Act. This is a 1951 statute which was last amended in 1957. As the Minister of Finance indicated in this chamber on October 17, the government has been giving some thought to a number of issues which, it can be appreciated, exist in a statute of this age. As the statute now stands, it brings considerable benefits to municipalities in all parts of Canada.
In this regard, I might note that total payments to British Columbia local governments and the province itself in respect of property in municipally unorganized territory are expected to reach about $15 million in the present fiscal year. The district of Surrey receives grants in lieu on various departmen-
October 31, 1978

tal properties. The grant for the 1977 taxation year was $147,804. No application has yet been received for 1978.
In so far as the Fraser River harbour commission is concerned, the property which they administer is not departmental property and is specifically excluded from the provisions of the Municipal Grants Act. The government does not contemplate that properties of this kind would be brought within a revised Municipal Grants Act within the foreseeable future because the various harbour commissions are joint, intergovernmental bodies. In many cases, they administer lands belonging to different levels of government.
It would seem somewhat anomalous for the federal government to establish a policy with respect to those lands under a port commission's jurisdiction which are federal, unless the same policy is to apply to the non-federal lands. However, this would raise a question as to why the federal government should establish a policy that would have very direct implications for the other governments involved, be they municipalities or provinces. In these circumstances, the government has decided to leave the matter of future grant policy to each port commission. It is hoped that this will result in the negotiation of arrangements which will be in the best interests of all concerned.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUPPLYING OF ARMS TO SOUTHERN AFRICA-POSITION TAKEN BY GREAT BRITAIN
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUPPLYING OF ARMS TO SOUTHERN AFRICA-POSITION TAKEN BY GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) yesterday was concerned with Great Britain's involvement in the supplying of arms and munitions to certain African states in high tension areas where such "aid" can only result in further violence and bloodshed. I wanted to know particularly whether the Canadian government has commented in any way to the United Kingdom with regard to this volatile situation, and the minister replied rather lamely in the negative. This does appear to be a case of silence being consent.
At any rate, the government does not appear to object to Britain involving herself in these African atrocities in precisely the same manner as the Russians and the Cubans, placing modern weaponry in the hands of tribal warriors whose main goal these days seems to be to kill anyone who disagrees with them, or even anyone they suspect might disagree with them.
It is a dangerous game, one which the communists have been playing for a long time in Africa and elsewhere. Britain and, by association, other members of the Commonwealth would be most unwise to get into this lopsided chess game at which the Russians are past masters. In that part of the world today, Britain is sadly outnumbered and it is foolhardy to think that sending a few guns-though in this case it is much more serious because we are talking about surface-to-air missiles and other such pieces of sophisticated equipment-to Zambia is going to thwart any plans being engineered by the communists.
Adjournment Debate
An arms build-up in Africa can only lead to tribal wars and genocide; civil wars, if you like. These in turn can spread across state borders, eventually involving any number of African states. Since Cuba has been highly visible in African affairs for some time-and it appears that our government has co-operated with Cuba in its efforts to get arms and men to that troubled continent in the past by allowing their war materiel to land in this country en route to Africa-and since it is common knowledge that the Soviet Union has been supplying various states and factions with war materiel for years, this is no game for the British who have enough problems at home and in Ireland.
By its commonwealth association and by its silent consent, the Canadian government is involving itself in African affairs along with Britain. This is foolhardy enough in itself, but really foolish when you stop to think of the odds stacked against anyone who confronts communist-backed forces in that part of the world now.
This government has been pouring money hand over fist into African countries, supposedly to feed starving millions of people. How much of that money is feeding the people and how much of it is buying bullets, bombs and back-up material from the communists? How much of that money is killing the very people it was intended to keep alive?
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the World Council of Churches has been giving aid to these terrorists. I was amazed on Sunday night to see the Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada on television admitting that he was only going by his conscience and was not concerned with what was actually going on. He had not made any effort to visit the area. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that 95 per cent of the people killed in Rhodesia by the guerrillas invading from Zambia are black people.
The minister said earlier today that he would need more specific information on Britain's involvement in African affairs. All he needs to do is read the same newspapers we all have access to. But he prefers to sit, wait for word from London, hoping and praying nervously all the while that these nasty things will pass away and Africa will settle down to a peaceful, pastoral picture once again. It seems to me he is proceeding in a very naive way.
I say to the minister that African people, in one part of that continent or another, have not known true peace in this entire century. There has always been some big nation from Europe sticking its thumb in to see what it could come up with. And Britain is back into the act, not as the empire builder she once was, but as a relatively minor member of a gang of misdirected moderns who will achieve nothing there but the building of a gigantic powder keg.
We must not forget that the Middle East problem also involves part of Africa-a big part of Africa in the north. So it is all part of the same grandiose chess game and it becomes increasingly and dangerously unstable every time one more non-African nation tries to get into the act.

October 31, 1978
Adjournment Debate
If Canada is seen to approve, silently or otherwise, British involvement in African affairs, then this country's position is jeopardized, whether we are seen as aligning ourselves with communist aggressors or simply doing nothing to persuade Britain from doing just that. If his government, as the minister says, really believes this kind of arms escalation must be brought to an end, then let us have some action on at least some strong words on the subject, not just a mouthful of excuses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) stated in the House on October 30 that he had had no conversations with the British Foreign Secretary regarding Britain's decision to send military supplies to Zambia. We would not, indeed, expect the British government to consult us on its transactions with a sovereign fellow member of the Commonwealth concerning its defence needs.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs added that, when he had more specific information, he would consider whether it was useful to the House to give a more detailed response. We are seeking confirmation of press and other reports that the military equipment sent to Zambia is for Zambia's defence needs, particularly air defence. According to reports, the supplies have included communications equipment, mine detectors and anti-aircraft guns, with the possibility of ground-to-air missiles to follow, and they have been supplied on condition that they are not handed on to the guerilla forces.
We also understand from reports that Dr. Owen has stated that there was no question of stationing British troops or aircraft in Zambia or of sending any equipment that could be used for any purpose other than the protection of Zambia.
As all hon. members will realize, the actions of the British government are related to the vexing Rhodesian question. For too many years the repressive Rhodesian regime has illegally exercised power in defiance of the international community and the situation has been in the forefront of unsolved international problems. The unacceptability of the illegal regime's policies and its intransigence in the face of international efforts to find solutions have through the years severely affected the neighbouring states. Incursions such as took place in recent weeks and particularly the raids into Zambia point up the need for all parties to get together to discuss peaceful ways to settle the affair without delay. Zambia is particularly vulnerable, both militarily and economically, to Rhodesian actions. It is unable to protect itself from the operation of the illegal regime's security forces. In addition, it has had to open its border to permit transhipment of vital supplies of fertilizer through Rhodesia.
It appears from all reports that the military supplies are indeed of a defensive nature and intended only for Zambia's defence should it be attacked. Until we have confirmation of the reports, however, we can make no further comment.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-POLICY REGARDING EXTENDED USE OF SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-POLICY REGARDING EXTENDED USE OF SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the face of it the social insurance number appears to be a simple and innocuous number to be given out as casually as you would give out your name. Unfortunately, the SIN number has become much more than that; it is becoming more and more a national identity number and the card a national identity card.
Think of all the occasions, sir, when the SIN number is used. It is used for registration at hospitals, schools, libraries, banks, insurance companies, and indeed it is now being used by the army as a regimental number. Youngsters playing pee-wee hockey are asked for their SIN numbers for the National Hockey Association's computer. Canadians must provide SIN to cash Canada Savings Bonds and SIN are a must on income tax returns. The school systems of Saskatchewan and Ontario use SIN for record keeping for students in senior grades. Motor vehicle drivers' records in Quebec, and hunting licences in Manitoba, are recorded by SIN.
Due to the ever-growing use of social insurance numbers in different agencies and departments at all levels of government and in the private field, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on October 27, 1978, the following. I asked her what the policy is regarding the extension of the use of social insurance numbers in a variety of ways so that they have now become glorified identification cards and numbers.
The question is important to Canadians for several reasons. First introduced in 1964, the Pearson government gave repeated assurances that numbers would not become national identity cards but would be used solely as social security numbers. Yet through the years, notwithstanding this firm undertaking, there has been extension of the system to most government departments.
My objections are twofold. The use of SIN has been so extended as to become a de facto national identity card, despite government assurances to the contrary. Secondly, this policy, whether overt or covert, has been adopted without a full examination and public debate of its merits and consequences. That is really the substance of my complaint in this matter. Maybe we will get to a single identification number in this country, but I suggest that the government has broken its word, broken the commitment made by Prime Minister Pearson and others not to let this policy be extended without first having a full debate on the implications of having a single identification number.
Closely related to these concerns is the problem of safeguards and laws to protect the confidentiality of the information in the computers. Information given for the purposes of one program, for example old age pensions, should not be transferred to other computers dealing with another program. Because of the increasing compatibility of the latest computers and their ability to communicate with each other, our social insurance number could then become a key which would open up our lives to the unscrupulous data bank manipulator.
October 31, 1978

Secondly, the access to the information in a file should be closely regulated to guard against abuse by government or other agency.
These concerns about our privacy in the face of new computer technology and increasing government are not abstract musings, in recognition of today's realities. I will give examples of some things that have happened according to testimony given by the assistant commissioner of the RCMP, Hank Jensen, to the McDonald commission into RCMP activities in June of this year. He gave some interesting information. He said that 50 per cent of all cases of false pretences made use of SIN cards. He pointed out that the problem relating to this false pretences percentage was due to lack of security surrounding SIN.
He illustrated the case of a Calgary man who had 109 SIN cards, 59 UIC claims and a monthly income of $33,000. He also told of a Montreal duo who used 60 SIN cards over a period of two months to collect $32,867 from the UIC and who had projected earnings of half a million dollars from their gainful unemployment had they not slipped up. Then there was the Winnipeg man who parlayed 25 SIN cards into $92,000 over 4'/2 years.
The minister missed the point of my question. We must have a public debate. Parliament must give its mandate to the expansion of the use of these numbers or we fail our responsibility in this House as individual members. The parliamentary secretary can take a message to the minister. I intend to pursue this matter until we get a satisfactory resolution of this very difficult and ominous problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-POLICY REGARDING EXTENDED USE OF SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has several times been suggested in this House that the government intends actively to promote the expanded use of social insurance numbers outside of social service programs by all levels of government. Such is not the government's policy, nor did the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) at any time say that it was. As she did say, however, the government
Adjournment Debate
is concerned to maintain tight control of the very large program of expenditure for which she is responsible as minister, and to that end the social insurance number is an indispensible tool.
As I said, the government is not trying to promote the extension of the use of the SIN outside the federal government. I am not saying, however, that the government will prohibit such use, or refuse to co-operate if a private sector organization, or one in another level of government, decides to make administrative use of the SIN. The holder of a social insurance number is at liberty to divulge it to those with whom he or she transacts business. Whether he or she does so or not is essentially a matter of negotiation between the parties. Any attempt on the part of the government to control or influence such negotiations would be intrusive, and probably ineffectual.
The use of the SIN in connection with the administration of unemployment insurance, the Canada Pension Plan, and the income tax is sanctioned by statute. In the context of those very large programs involving millions of Canadians, effective administration is impossible without a unique identifier for each citizen involved. Large business firms, other levels of government and, indeed, other departments of the federal government doing business across the country experience the same administrative need. It should therefore occasion no surprise if these organizations ask a person with whom they deal for an identifier which distinguishes him or her from all others of similar name.
As to the use of the social insurance number within the federal government outside the area of "social service programs", such use has, of course, been recognized since parliament amended the Income Tax Act in 1967 to provide for the use of the SIN on income tax returns. Other departments also use the SIN as a matter of administrative practice, in the same manner as do firms in the private sector.
